newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU sees extended international presence in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: EU sees extended international presence in Bosnia.

text.p: The international community will probably need to maintain a civilian and military presence in Bosnia for at least two more years, the EU signalled at the weekend.
"Everything so far has been easy compared with what lies ahead," Carl Bildt, the international community's High Representative in Bosnia, told reporters on Sunday.

European Union foreign ministers, ending a two-day informal meeting in the southwestern Irish town of Tralee on Sunday, were in broad agreement on the need for a period of consolidation in Bosnia to follow the withdrawal of NATO-led forces in December.
"I think it is evident there is going to be a long-term engagement...both military and civilian," Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring, whose country is current EU president, told a news conference.

Ministers from the 15-nation bloc endorsed the idea of a two-year peace consolidation period for economic reconstruction, promotion of human rights, dealing with refugees, and ensuring regional stabilisation and arms control.

"In Bosnia, you don't have self-supported stability so the civil implementation of the Dayton peace agreements will have to be safeguarded from the outside," German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said.
"The view is growing that the institutions concerned (with Bosnia) -- the United Nations, NATO, the Europeans -- will decide that such outside help would be necessary," he said.
British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind also said a continued presence in Bosnia was likely, but added that it should not be an open-ended commitment.
The United Nations has had troops in Cyprus for years on end without any discernible progress, he said.
Bildt said there was general agreement on the idea of setting a two-year limit on the terms of officials to be elected in Bosnia on September 14.
"There is a wide consensus that we should head for new elections in 1998," he told reporters.
Bildt, who had briefed the ministers on Saturday, said there was a need for a security force with substantial capabilities to remain in Bosnia for the period.
He and others said, however, that it would not need to be anything like as large as the current NATO-led implementation force, IFOR.
Bildt said the reason for a continued international presence was that the coming elections marked only the end of one period in Bosnia's emergence from war.
Diplomats said the ministers had been keen to talk about a two-year period as a way of showing the various parties in Bosnia that the EU planned to remain engaged long after elections.
Spring also said Ireland had agreed to host a one-day conference on September 28 to win cash and manpower pledges for training a police force for post-war Bosnia.
Some 40 countries would be invited to the talks to get pledges of support for what Western states see as a cornerstone of Bosnia's recovery from civil war.
